description: Hang from a sturdy edge by your fingertips and start the clock. Your finger hang time exposes the finger tendons and their pulley system, the smallest cables climbers trust with their lives. Learn why full-hand gripping is backwards, how the pulleys multiply force, and the careful protocol that builds them.

beats.text: A STURDY EDGE. LOW AND SAFE.

scenes.narration: Find a sturdy edge you can hang from with just your fingers: the top of a solid door, a thick ledge, a strong beam, something that will not move, close enough to the ground that your feet can catch you. Curl your fingertips over it, no palm, no thumb, and lift your feet. Start the clock. How long can your fingers alone hold your body before the grip peels open? That time is your FINGER HANG TEST. It measures the smallest and most overloaded cable system in your body, the finger tendons and the pulleys that guide them, the same system rock climbers trust with their lives. Keep it safe: low edge, soft landing, and any sharp finger pain ends the test instantly. Write your seconds down. At the end I will tell you what they mean, and why normal grip training barely touches this system.

scenes.label: SECONDS OF FINGERTIP HANG
scenes.narration: Here is the line. TWENTY seconds of clean fingertip hang means your finger tendons and pulleys are sharing load like a trained system. Under eight is where almost everyone starts, because daily life never asks your fingers to do this. Over thirty, you are in climber territory, holding bodyweight on cables thinner than pencils, and that strength is built slowly, respectfully, and on purpose.
scenes.sub: under 8: untrained pulleys - 8 to 19: building - over 30: climber territory

lines: Pulleys keep them on the bone.
beats.title: CABLES AND PULLEYS

scenes.narration: Here is the anatomy that makes climbers obsessed. Your fingers contain almost no muscle. The muscles that close them live in your forearm, and they pull long tendons that run through your wrist, across your palm, and out to the fingertips, like brake cables through a bicycle frame. A cable pulled around a bend wants to lift away from the bone, so your fingers are wrapped in PULLEYS, rings of tough tissue that pin each tendon down and keep it tracking. When you fingertip-hang, your entire bodyweight hangs from those cables and the little rings guiding them. It is the highest force-to-size ratio anywhere in your body. This is why the finger system cannot be trained like a biceps. It is precision hardware, and it answers to patient, progressive load, not enthusiasm. The pulley system has one more feature that should earn your respect: it has almost no backup. A finger has no spare tendon waiting in reserve, and the pulleys that guide it are nourished poorly compared to muscle, which is why they heal slowly when they are hurt. Every climber who has ignored a sore finger has learned the calendar lesson the hard way: weeks of patience, or months of repair. Train like the tissue is precious, because anatomically, it is.

Now the backwards part. Most grip training is full-hand squeezing: grippers, balls, thick bars. That work is shared across the whole hand, the palm, the thumb, big surfaces, and the finger tendons coast in the crowd. The fingertip hang removes every helper. Four fingers, open hand, cables and pulleys carrying the load with nowhere to hide. Climbers learned this decades ago: finger strength is specific to the position you train, and the open-hand position, fingers extended over an edge, loads the pulley system most honestly and most safely. This specificity is why strong gym grips can still peel off a ledge in five seconds. Different system, different test, different training. You cannot squeeze your way to pulley strength. You have to hang, carefully, in the position itself. There is a simple test of honesty built into the edge itself. Either the fingers hold or they peel. No momentum, no bounce, no partial credit. Few exercises in this series grade you as cleanly as this one does.

Follow the fingers outward and they are the interface between you and every hold in your training. The bar in your dead hang, the towel in your towel hang, the edge of any wall or branch: your body reaches the world through these cables first. When the fingers are the weak link, every upstream muscle waits, underused. When the pulleys are wired, grip stops being the reason sets end early, and your back, arms, and shoulders finally get their full training dose. This is also why climbers, who are often light and lean, display some of the most extreme strength-to-weight ratios in sport. They did not build bigger engines first. They built the interface, the tiny cables that connect engine to world.

And this test, more than any other on this channel, is rigged for the light guy. The load on your pulleys is your bodyweight, full stop. Every kilo you do not carry is load the tiny cables do not have to hold, which means you can train the position longer, more often, with cleaner form. There is a reason elite climbers look like you and not like bodybuilders: the sport selected for the exact build you already have. The heavy guy's fingers peel in seconds and his training dose stays tiny. Yours can stretch into real sessions. On this one test, being skinny is not the thing you overcome. It is the qualifying advantage.

Hang with me, carefully. Fingertips on the edge, feet light on the floor taking some weight if you need it, fifteen seconds of work, thirty of rest, five rounds. Comfortable effort only. Any sharp pain, we stop. Go.

beats.text: WRONG 1: MAX HANGS IN WEEK ONE

scenes.narration: Now, stop doing it wrong, and with fingers this section matters most. Wrong one: max hangs in week one. Pulleys are the slowest adapters in this whole series, and a maximal load on cold, untrained rings is how climbers get injured. Wrong two: only full-hand gripping and expecting fingertip strength to appear by magic. Wrong three: training fingers hard every day. This tissue wants full recovery between real sessions, two or three quality days a week, not seven sloppy ones. Wrong four: the crimp position, fingertips bent sharply backward under load, before months of open-hand base. Wrong five: ignoring a tender pulley because it is small. Doing it right is humble: open-hand hangs at an effort you could repeat, feet helping at first, rest days respected, progress measured in seconds per month. And the rule is absolute here: a pop, a sharp pain, or a finger that stays sore goes to a professional, ideally one who knows climbing injuries. These cables are small. Treat them like they matter, because they carry everything.

scenes.label: RETEST THE FINGER HANG
scenes.narration: So, your number. Under EIGHT: the pulleys are untrained, which is the human default, not a defect. Eight to nineteen: the system is learning, and careful hangs will move you steadily. Over TWENTY: your fingers hold what most people's whole hands cannot, and that is a genuinely rare strength. Progress here is measured in seconds per month, and that is winning, not failing. Same edge, same rules in thirty days. Put today's seconds in the comments. Just the number. The climbers in the thread will know exactly what it cost.
scenes.sub: same edge, open hand, feet ready to catch you

scenes.narration: Your fingers were never weak. They were uninvited, left out of every training plan you ever followed. Give the pulleys thirty careful days and bring me the new number.
